title: 02. Threading: Day 1 — Threading Fundamentals
summary: Rule of thumb: Network/disk heavy, many connections → asyncio; CPU heavy, few workers → multiprocessing; CPU heavy, needs shared state → multiprocessing.Manager; Legacy sync library you can't rewrite → threading (or run_in_executor in…
objectives: Explain what a thread is and how Python threads differ from OS threads.
Describe the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and predict when threading will and won't speed up code.
Walk through the full thread lifecycle: new → runnable → running → blocked → dead.
Spawn threads using both threading.Thread(target=...) and the Thread subclass pattern.
Diagnose a race condition and explain why shared mutable state breaks naive threading.
Use threading.local() to keep per-thread state isolated.

sections.body:

```
                         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                         │       What is the bottleneck?        │
                         └──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                        │
                ┌───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
                │                                               │
        ┌───────▼───────┐                               ┌───────▼───────┐
        │   I/O bound   │                               │   CPU bound   │

        │  disk, DB)    │                               │  processing)  │

                │                                               │
        ┌───────┴───────┐                               ┌───────┴───────┐
        │ Low overhead, │                               │ True parallel │
        │ 1000s of ops  │                               │ Bypasses GIL  │
        │               │                               │               │
        │   asyncio ✅  │                               │ multiprocessing│
        │  (best)       │                               │     ✅ (best)  │
        │               │                               │               │
        │ threading     │                               │ threading ❌  │
        │ (if lib is    │                               │ (GIL blocks)  │
        │  sync)        │                               │               │
        └───────────────┘                               └───────────────┘
```

**Rule of thumb:**
- **Network/disk heavy, many connections** → `asyncio`
- **CPU heavy, few workers** → `multiprocessing`
- **CPU heavy, needs shared state** → `multiprocessing.Manager`
- **Legacy sync library you can't rewrite** → `threading` (or `run_in_executor` in async)

sections.title: Theory & Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### 1. What is a Thread?

A **thread** is the smallest unit of execution that the OS can schedule on a CPU core. Multiple threads share the **same process memory space**, which makes creating a thread ~100× cheaper than creating a process and lets threads communicate instantly through shared variables — but also opens the door to **race conditions**.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────── Process (one Python interpreter) ─────────┐
│                                                                               │
│   Shared heap:  modules, lists, dicts, file handles, sockets, globals        │
│                                                                               │
│   ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐                          │
│   │  Thread A   │  │  Thread B   │  │  Thread C   │   Each thread has its    │
│   │  ─────────  │  │  ─────────  │  │  ─────────  │   own stack + registers  │
│   │  stack      │  │  stack      │  │  stack      │   + instruction pointer  │
│   │  locals     │  │  locals     │  │  locals     │                          │
│   └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘                          │
│          │                │                │                                  │
│          └────────────────┴────────────────┘   All access shared heap       │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2. The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)

CPython protects its internal data structures with a single mutex called the **GIL**. Only **one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time**, regardless of how many CPU cores you have.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T1 as Thread 1
    participant T2 as Thread 2
    participant GIL as GIL
    participant CPU as CPU core
    Note over T1,T2: Both runnable, but only one runs Python bytecode
    T1->>GIL: Acquire
    GIL-->>T1: Granted
    T1->>CPU: Execute bytecode (5ms tick)
    Note over T1: After 5ms or I/O, GIL released
    T1->>GIL: Release (forced)
    T2->>GIL: Acquire
    GIL-->>T2: Granted
    T2->>CPU: Execute bytecode (5ms tick)
    T2->>GIL: Release
    T1->>GIL: Acquire
```

**The GIL is released when:**
- A thread does blocking I/O (`socket.recv`, `file.read`, `time.sleep`).
- A C extension explicitly releases it (NumPy, hashlib, etc.).
- After ~5ms (the `sys.setswitchinterval` default) of pure Python execution.

**Consequences:**
- Threading **does** speed up I/O-bound code (network, disk, DB).
- Threading **does NOT** speed up CPU-bound Python code — threads serialize on the GIL.
- Multiprocessing bypasses the GIL because each process has its own interpreter + GIL.

### 3. Thread Lifecycle

```
        ┌──────────┐  Thread() created
        │   NEW    │
        └────┬─────┘
             │ .start()
             ▼
        ┌──────────┐
        │ RUNNABLE │  ← waiting for OS scheduler
        └────┬─────┘
             │ scheduled
             ▼
        ┌──────────┐
        │ RUNNING  │  ← executing bytecode
        └────┬─────┘
             │ blocking call (I/O, lock.acquire)
             ▼
        ┌──────────┐
        │ BLOCKED  │  ← waiting for resource
        └────┬─────┘
             │ resource ready
             ▼
        ┌──────────┐
        │ RUNNABLE │  ← back to scheduler queue
        └────┬─────┘
             │ run() returns / target completes
             ▼
        ┌──────────┐
        │   DEAD   │  ← .join() returns
        └──────────┘
```

### 4. Race Condition: The Classic Counter

Two threads incrementing `counter += 1` 1,000,000 times each. Expected: 2,000,000. Actual (varies): anywhere from 1,003,217 to 1,987,402.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T1
    participant T2
    participant Mem as counter (in memory)
    Mem->>Mem: counter = 0
    T1->>Mem: READ counter → 0
    Note over T1: register holds 0
    T1->>T1: ADD 1 → 1   (not yet written!)
    T2->>Mem: READ counter → 0  (still 0!)
    T2->>T2: ADD 1 → 1
    T2->>Mem: WRITE 1
    T1->>Mem: WRITE 1
    Note over Mem: counter == 1, but should be 2 ❌
```

The fix (Day 2): use a `Lock` so only one thread can do the read-modify-write atomically.

sections.title: Example 1 — Basic Thread with target= and args=
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 1: Spawn a thread with target function and arguments."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import threading
import time
from typing import Final

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(threadName)s] %(levelname)s: %(message)s",
)
logger: Final = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def worker(name: str, iterations: int) -> None:
    """Log a greeting `iterations` times with a small delay."""
    for i in range(iterations):
        logger.info("Hello from %s — iteration %d", name, i)
        time.sleep(0.05)

def main() -> None:
    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("alpha", 3), name="Worker-Alpha")
    t.start()
    t.join()  # block until the thread finishes
    logger.info("Worker finished, exiting main.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Key points:** `start()` schedules the thread; `join()` blocks the caller until it terminates. Pass positional args via `args=`, keyword args via `kwargs=`.

sections.title: Example 2 — Thread Subclass with run()
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 2: Subclass Thread for reusable, stateful workers."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import threading
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(threadName)s: %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass
class CountingThread(threading.Thread):
    """A thread that counts to `limit` and exposes its final count."""

    limit: int = 5
    delay: float = 0.1
    _count: int = field(default=0, init=False)

    def __init__(self, limit: int, delay: float = 0.1, name: str | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(name=name)
        self.limit: int = limit
        self.delay: float = delay
        self._count: int = 0

    def run(self) -> None:
        """Entry point — called by start()."""
        for i in range(self.limit):
            self._count = i + 1
            logger.info("count=%d", self._count)
            time.sleep(self.delay)

    @property
    def count(self) -> int:
        """Read-only access to the current count."""
        return self._count

def main() -> None:
    t = CountingThread(limit=5, delay=0.1, name="Counter")
    t.start()
    t.join()
    logger.info("Final count reported: %d", t.count)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**When to subclass:** when the thread owns significant state or you want to override `run()` with reusable logic. Otherwise prefer `target=` — it's simpler and testable.

sections.title: Example 3 — Daemon Threads and join(timeout=)
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 3: Daemon threads vs joinable threads, plus join with timeout."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import threading
import time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(threadName)s: %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def heartbeat(interval: float) -> None:
    """Run forever, logging a heartbeat."""
    while True:
        logger.info("♥ heartbeat")
        time.sleep(interval)

def short_task(seconds: float) -> None:
    """A finite task that returns after `seconds`."""
    time.sleep(seconds)
    logger.info("short_task done")

def main() -> None:
    # Daemon threads are killed abruptly when the main thread exits.
    daemon = threading.Thread(target=heartbeat, args=(0.5,), name="daemon", daemon=True)
    daemon.start()

    worker = threading.Thread(target=short_task, args=(1.2,), name="worker")
    worker.start()

    # Wait at most 0.5s for worker — will time out.
    worker.join(timeout=0.5)
    if worker.is_alive():
        logger.warning("worker still running after 0.5s timeout — continuing anyway")

    # Wait properly now.
    worker.join()
    logger.info("main exiting; daemon thread will be killed")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Key points:**
- `daemon=True` ⇒ Python won't wait for the thread at interpreter shutdown.
- `join(timeout=)` returns even if the thread is still alive — check `is_alive()`.

sections.title: Example 4 — Race Condition Demo
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 4: Demonstrate a real race condition on a shared counter."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import threading

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class Counter:
    """A deliberately unsafe counter."""
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.value: int = 0

    def increment(self, times: int) -> None:
        for _ in range(times):
            # NOT atomic: read-modify-write across multiple bytecodes.
            self.value += 1

def main() -> None:
    counter = Counter()
    N_THREADS = 10
    N_INCREMENTS = 100_000
    threads = [
        threading.Thread(target=counter.increment, args=(N_INCREMENTS,), name=f"T{i}")
        for i in range(N_THREADS)
    ]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    expected = N_THREADS * N_INCREMENTS
    logger.warning("expected=%d  actual=%d  lost=%d",
                   expected, counter.value, expected - counter.value)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Run it 5 times.** You'll get a different `actual` every time — that's the signature of a race condition. Day 2 fixes it with `Lock`.

sections.title: Example 5 — Thread Identification: name, ident, native_id
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 5: Inspect a thread's identity via name / ident / native_id."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import threading
import time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def show_identities() -> None:
    me = threading.current_thread()
    logger.info("name=%-12s ident=%-6s native_id=%s",
                me.name, me.ident, me.native_id)
    time.sleep(0.2)

def main() -> None:
    logger.info("main thread: ident=%s", threading.current_thread().ident)
    threads = [
        threading.Thread(target=show_identities, name=f"worker-{i}")
        for i in range(3)
    ]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    # Enumerate every thread still alive (includes main thread).
    for t in threading.enumerate():
        logger.info("alive: name=%s daemon=%s", t.name, t.daemon)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Key points:**
- `name` is for humans (logs, debugging).
- `ident` is a small integer reused after a thread dies — don't use as a key.
- `native_id` is the OS-level TID — useful for `top -H`, `py-spy`, profilers.

sections.title: Example 6 — threading.local() for Per-Thread State
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 6: Use threading.local() so each thread has its own copy of state."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import random
import threading
import time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(threadName)s: %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# Each thread that touches `local_state` gets its OWN attribute namespace.
local_state: threading.local = threading.local()

def worker() -> None:
    # Set per-thread values — invisible to other threads.
    local_state.request_id = random.randint(1000, 9999)
    local_state.user = threading.current_thread().name

    for i in range(3):
        # Access via the same object — but each thread sees its own data.
        logger.info("request_id=%s user=%s i=%d",
                    local_state.request_id, local_state.user, i)
        time.sleep(0.1)

def main() -> None:
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, name=f"req-{i}") for i in range(3)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    # main thread has never set request_id — accessing it raises AttributeError.
    try:
        _ = local_state.request_id
    except AttributeError:
        logger.info("main thread has no request_id (expected)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Why this matters:** `local()` is how frameworks like Flask/SQLAlchemy keep per-request DB connections thread-isolated without passing them through every function call.

sections.title: Example 7 — Thread-Safe Logging (One File, Many Writers)
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 7: Configure logging so multiple threads write to one file safely."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import logging.handlers
import threading
import time
from pathlib import Path

LOG_PATH = Path("/tmp/threadsafe.log")

def configure_logging() -> None:
    """Set up a QueueHandler + QueueListener so writes are serialized."""
    LOG_PATH.unlink(missing_ok=True)

    file_handler = logging.FileHandler(LOG_PATH, mode="a", encoding="utf-8")
    file_handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(
        "%(asctime)s [%(threadName)s] %(levelname)s: %(message)s"
    ))

    listener = logging.handlers.QueueListener(
        logging.handlers.QueueHandler([]).__class__().queue  # placeholder, see below
        if False else None,  # placeholder disabled — real setup below
        file_handler,
    )

    # NOTE: the cleaner way:
    queue: typing.Any  # actual queue created below
    import queue as _q
    real_queue: _q.Queue[logging.LogRecord] = _q.Queue()
    queue_handler = logging.handlers.QueueHandler(real_queue)
    queue_handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(message)s"))
    root = logging.getLogger()
    root.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    root.addHandler(queue_handler)

    real_listener = logging.handlers.QueueListener(real_queue, file_handler, respect_handler_level=True)
    real_listener.start()

    # Stash listener so it can be stopped at exit.
    logging._queue_listener = real_listener  # type: ignore[attr-defined]

def worker(task_id: int) -> None:
    logging.info("task %d starting", task_id)
    time.sleep(0.05)
    logging.info("task %d done", task_id)

def main() -> None:
    import typing
    configure_logging()
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,), name=f"T{i}") for i in range(5)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    listener: logging.handlers.QueueListener = logging._queue_listener  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    listener.stop()
    print(f"Log written to {LOG_PATH}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Why `QueueHandler`?** A plain `FileHandler` is *technically* thread-safe in CPython (the GIL serializes `write()` calls), but lines can still interleave mid-flush on some platforms. `QueueHandler` sends records to a single listener thread — guaranteed order, no interleaving, and zero I/O on worker threads.

sections.title: Day 1 Cheat Sheet
sections.body:
| Concept | Snippet |
|---|---|
| Spawn | `t = threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(x,), name="T1")` |
| Start | `t.start()` |
| Wait | `t.join()` or `t.join(timeout=5)` |
| Daemon | `Thread(..., daemon=True)` |
| Identity | `t.name`, `t.ident`, `t.native_id` |
| Enumerate | `threading.enumerate()` |
| Per-thread state | `local = threading.local(); local.x = 1` |
| GIL switch interval | `sys.getswitchinterval()` (default 0.005s) |

**Tomorrow (Day 2):** We fix the race condition with `Lock`, learn all the synchronization primitives (`Semaphore`, `Event`, `Condition`, `Barrier`), and graduate to `ThreadPoolExecutor` for clean concurrent I/O.
